title: Square-root logarithmic approximation for metric labeling
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal:
Do there exist absolute constants \(C,K\ge1\), an integer \(d\ge1\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm such that on every metric-labeling instance of binary length \(L\) with \(k\ge1\) labels, every execution halts within \(K(L+1)^d\) bit steps and outputs a labeling \(f\) satisfying
\[
\Pr\!\left[\operatorname{cost}(f)\le C\sqrt{\log_2(k+2)}\,\operatorname{OPT}\right]\ge\tfrac23?
\]
The input graph, nonnegative rational edge weights and assignment costs, and full rational metric on the labels are arbitrary. The output is always a feasible labeling; \(\operatorname{OPT}\) is the least cost of any labeling.
definitions:
An instance has a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=[n]\) and \(n\ge0\), and label set \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), with \(k\ge1\). Every edge \(\{u,v\}\in E\) has a nonnegative rational weight \(w_{uv}\). For each vertex \(v\) and label \(i\) there is a nonnegative rational assignment cost \(c(v,i)\). A metric is supplied as the entire \(k\)-by-\(k\) matrix \(d\): its entries are finite nonnegative rationals, \(d(i,j)=d(j,i)\), \(d(i,j)=0\) if and only if \(i=j\), and \(d(i,j)\le d(i,\ell)+d(\ell,j)\) for all labels. There is no dimension, embedding, graph-structure or distance-ratio promise.

A feasible labeling is a function \(f:V\to[k]\), with cost
\[
\operatorname{cost}(f)=\sum_{v\in V}c(v,f(v))+
\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}w_{uv}\,d(f(u),f(v)).
\]
Each undirected edge is counted once. Define \(\operatorname{OPT}=\min_{f:V\to[k]}\operatorname{cost}(f)\); this is a finite minimum over \(k^n\) possibilities. For the empty graph the cost and optimum are zero. More generally the multiplicative guarantee applies also when \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\), requiring zero output cost on the successful event. No infinite forbidden-assignment penalties or label capacities are part of the input.

Use an explicit binary encoding listing \(n,k\), the edges with endpoints and weights, all \(nk\) assignment costs, and the full metric matrix in a fixed order. Each rational is a binary nonnegative numerator over a binary positive denominator, with length delimiters; reduced form is optional. \(L\) is the total bit length, including all numbers and delimiters. Any malformed input may be rejected; the accuracy condition applies to valid metric instances. An output lists one label for each vertex.

The algorithm is one probabilistic Turing machine with independent fair random bits, no advice and no oracle. Its finite description, time exponent and constants are independent of \(n,k\), the graph and all numeric values. Every input and every random tape satisfy the time bound, including tapes on which the approximation fails. All preprocessing, arithmetic on rational encodings and output writing are charged. The probability is over the algorithm's coins separately for each fixed input. The constant \(C\) is chosen before the input and need not have a prescribed numerical value. The number of labels is part of the input, rather than a fixed parameter.

This is a claim about algorithms for the integer labeling objective, not a request that a particular linear-programming relaxation have that integrality gap. Algorithms can use any technique meeting the stated bit complexity.

context_blocks.text: Local assignment costs prefer particular labels, while edge penalties encourage neighboring objects to receive nearby labels. Arbitrary label metrics make the objective more general than uniform-label partitioning.
The known logarithmic algorithm provides an upper benchmark. Special metrics, such as a uniform metric or a line, allow stronger guarantees but do not settle the general target.
Conditional hardness motivates the square-root-logarithmic scale. It does not by itself refute an algorithm at the scale asked here, and an LP gap alone is not a lower bound against every algorithm.

why: Close a major gap for a general labeling objective linking metric geometry and approximation.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the stated uniform existence claim or its logical negation. An affirmative solution must prove feasibility, the per-input probability guarantee and worst-case polynomial bit time. An approximation with a larger asymptotic factor, a result for a special label metric or graph family, or a bound only for one relaxation does not decide this proposition. A complexity-theoretic assumption must be explicit, and a conditional negative result establishes only its conditional claim.

references.locator: Journal abstract: conditional constant-factor and almost-square-root-logarithmic inapproximability; not a refutation of the selected square-root-logarithmic guarantee.

progress.text: The primary paper gives an \(O(\log k)\) approximation for general metrics and stronger guarantees in specified special cases; Theorem 5.3 controls its relaxation.

The primary hardness paper excludes constant-factor approximation under P different from NP and gives a stronger conditional near-square-root-logarithmic lower bound. The precise hardness model and assumptions remain distinct from this randomized algorithmic existence claim.

Its cost combines vertex assignment costs with distances between labels across weighted edges.
The selected target is a randomized polynomial-time approximation growing only as the square root of the logarithm of the number of labels.
